summary.text: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther of a plant to the stigma of a plant, later enabling fertilisation and the production of seeds.
Insects such as bees, beetles and butterflies, as well as birds, bats, water, wind and even plants themselves, can carry the pollen.
In flowering plants, a pollen grain on the stigma grows a tube down the style to an ovary, and its two gametes travel down that tube.

facts.label: Pollinating agents
facts.value: Animals, wind, water and even plants themselves

facts.label: Self-pollination
facts.value: Can happen within a closed flower or between flowers on one plant

facts.label: Double fertilisation
facts.value: One male nucleus joins the egg, the other joins the polar bodies

facts.label: Studied by
facts.value: Christian Konrad Sprengel addressed it in the 18th century

items.prompt: A beetle carries pollen from one flower's anther to a stigma. What does this make possible later?

options.label: Fertilisation and the production of seeds
The rooting of the plant in new soil
A clone of the plant without any gametes
The pollen turning into the stigma

items.explain: Pollination moves pollen from an anther to a stigma, later enabling fertilisation and seed production.

items.prompt: A flower stays shut its whole life, yet pollination still takes place. How is that possible?

options.label: Pollen enters through the roots of the plant
Pollination is never needed for seeds to form
Only wind can ever reach a shut flower
Pollen can move within the flower itself

items.explain: Self-pollination can occur within a closed flower, or between flowers on the same plant.

items.prompt: A plant breeder deliberately dusts pollen from one species onto the flowers of another. What might result?

options.label: Seeds that can never form
Hybrid offspring
A clone of the pollen parent
Pollen that grows into the new plant

items.explain: When pollination occurs between species it can produce hybrid offspring, in nature and in plant breeding work.

items.prompt: A pollen grain lands on the receiving surface of a flower. How do its gametes reach the ovule?

options.label: They swim through the style on their own
The wind blows them down the style
The ovary pulls the whole pollen grain inside
The grain grows a tube that carries them down

items.explain: In angiosperms the pollen grain germinates on the stigma and grows a pollen tube down the style, and its gametes travel down the tube.

items.prompt: A pollen grain sits in its anther and is not germinating there. Why not?

options.label: It is severely dehydrated, and germination only follows rehydration
It has no male gametes until it lands on a stigma
The wall of the anther blocks any tube from forming
It must first be fertilised before it can sprout

items.explain: Pollen is severely dehydrated and germinates only after rehydration, which stops premature germination in the anther.

items.prompt: A pine's ovule sits exposed on a cone scale. How does this change the pollen's trip compared with a flower?

options.label: It needs no pollen at all to make a seed
Wind can never carry pollen to it
The pollen need not penetrate carpel tissue to reach the ovule
It must pass through an ovary first

items.explain: In gymnosperms the ovule is exposed rather than enclosed in a carpel, so penetration of carpel tissue is unnecessary.
